chunks: "An interrupt service routine, or ISR, is the function that runs when an interrupt occurs.
It's different from a normal function because I never call it: the hardware does, by looking up its address in the vector table when the interrupt request is accepted.
It takes no arguments and returns nothing, because there's no caller to give it anything. A typical ISR does a few things in a fixed order.
It identifies the cause, if the vector is shared. It clears the interrupt flag so the request doesn't immediately fire again.
It does the minimum time-critical work, like reading the received byte into a buffer, reading a sensor register, or updating a counter.
And it signals the main code, usually by setting a volatile flag or posting to a queue, so the real processing happens outside the interrupt.
The rules I keep: it has to be short and fast, because other interrupts wait while it runs, it can't block or wait, and anything shared with main code has to be volatile and accessed safely.
On a Cortex-M the ISR is just a plain C function with the right name; on an AVR you use a special ISR macro so the compiler saves the registers and ends with a return-from-interrupt."
